bull_thesis:
The bull case can no longer rest on the approval, because the approval already happened. It rests on Viridian converting a genuinely differentiated drug into revenue against an incumbent that has had the market to itself for six years, with roughly a billion dollars of cash to fund the attempt.

On 26 June 2026 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration cleared Lumvoa (veligrotug-vvze) for thyroid eye disease, four days ahead of its 30 June target decision date, with no advisory committee and no rejection letter. The approved wording is better than the base case: it is the first drug in its class labelled for the disease regardless of how active or long-standing it is, and the first to show a statistically significant effect on both double-vision improvement and complete resolution across the full disease spectrum. Among trial patients with double vision at the start, 59% improved and 49% saw it resolve completely, against 20% and 12% on placebo. The treatment course is five infusions every three weeks over about twelve weeks, against the eight infusions over roughly 24 weeks required by Amgen's Tepezza. For a patient sitting in an infusion chair, and for the clinic scheduling those chairs, that is a visible advantage rather than a statistical one. Viridian launched the same week with its sales, market access and patient-services organisation already hired and its supply chain already standing, exactly as management promised on the 5 May 2026 first-quarter call, and priced the course at about $450,000 - broadly in line with the incumbent rather than undercutting it, which protects the class economics.

The market it is entering already works. Tepezza built roughly $2 billion of annual demand with no competition since 2020, which means physicians recognise the disease, insurers pay for the class, and infusion economics are settled. Viridian is competing for demand, not creating it. Second entrants into proven, reimbursed rare-disease markets with a better label usually do take meaningful share, and the sell side agrees: on approval Wedbush lifted its target to $43, Goldman Sachs to $39, Truist to $38 and RBC to $35, leaving seventeen analysts averaging $36.13 against a $19.70 share price at the 27 July 2026 close.

The balance sheet buys the time this needs, and it is stronger than a casual reading suggests. Cash stood at $762.2 million on 31 March 2026; the company then raised $350 million gross in early May - 7,352,942 shares at $17.00 plus $225 million of 1.75% convertible notes due 2032 struck at about $24.65 - for net proceeds near $334.7 million, and collected a further $75 million approval milestone from its royalty partner DRI Healthcare in late June. Net of one launch-weighted quarter of burn, cash today is roughly $1.0 billion, or about $790 million net of the 2032 notes. That is roughly $6.50 to $7.00 a share against a $19.70 price, it was raised opportunistically before the binary event rather than after it, and it means no emergency equity issue is required for at least two years.

Strip the cash out and the operating business carries an enterprise value near $1.4 billion, against a franchise that could reach $1.4 to $1.5 billion of combined peak annual sales if Lumvoa approaches $900 million worldwide and the under-the-skin follow-on, elegrobart, adds $500 to $600 million after its planned first-quarter 2027 approval filing. Both of elegrobart's late-stage trials met their goals, so the second product is a weaker drug than hoped rather than a failed one, and a European decision in 2027 adds a second geography. The conditions this case depends on are narrow and checkable: broad insurance coverage arriving inside management's six-to-nine-month guidance, infusion sites actually switching, and the elegrobart filing landing on time.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is simply that the market has already seen the good outcome and refused to pay for it. Approval arrived early and clean on 26 June 2026, and a month later the shares sit at $19.70 - below the 200-day average of $24.03 and roughly 43% under the 52-week high of $34.29. When the best version of a binary event does not pay, the market is pricing something the event did not address.

That something is dated 30 March 2026. Viridian reported topline results from REVEAL-1, the late-stage trial of elegrobart, the under-the-skin version of the same drug mechanism, and the stock fell roughly a third in a single session. The trial met its main goal, but the effect size did not travel: 54% proptosis response on the every-four-weeks dose and 63% on the every-eight-weeks dose against an unusually high 18% placebo rate at week 24, versus 70% against 5% placebo at week 15 for the approved infused drug. That is a placebo-adjusted gap of roughly 36 to 45 percentage points against roughly 64. The self-administered format is the one that was supposed to carry this franchise over the long run in a chronic disease, and it is materially weaker than the drug it was meant to replace. That is an impairment of terminal value, not a sentiment wobble, and it explains why an approval three months later could not lift the stock back.

Meanwhile the spending is fixed and the revenue is not. The company lost $104.9 million in the first quarter of 2026 on $141 thousand of revenue - $77.6 million of research spending and $38.7 million of selling and administrative - with a full commercial organisation hired ahead of a launch that had not yet started. Management itself guides to broad insurance coverage taking six to nine months, which means the ramp does not really begin until roughly December 2026 through March 2027, and payer contracting against a six-year incumbent usually places the newcomer behind it on formulary first. Amgen has both the resources and the motive to defend roughly $2 billion of annual demand.

The financing that de-risked the balance sheet also diluted the upside. The May offerings took the common count from 102.5 million to roughly 110 million, convertible preferred stock adds about 14.3 million common-equivalent shares, and the 2032 notes add roughly 9.1 million more above $24.65 - a fully diluted count near 134 million against the roughly 102 million most published targets were built on. On top of that, about 7.5% of U.S. franchise sales is permanently owed to a royalty partner. Both of those come straight out of the per-share bull case, and neither is reflected in the $36 average target.

The confirmation to watch for: a second-quarter report around 5 August 2026 with no visible prescription momentum or coverage wins; a payer decision that puts Lumvoa behind Tepezza on formulary; a slower-than-guided coverage build into 2027; or any slippage in the first-quarter 2027 approval filing for elegrobart. Any of those and the operating business gets marked back toward its cash.
sop_bull: About $30 a share, with a range of $28 to $32 - meaningfully below the $36.13 street average and the $35 our board carried, because those were built on a smaller share count and before the royalty. Built from parts: (1) Lumvoa, the approved infused drug, reaching roughly $900 million of peak worldwide sales - a plausible share of a class Amgen has already grown to about $2 billion annually - less the roughly 7.5% royalty on U.S. sales owed to DRI Healthcare, valued at about 3 times net peak sales for a de-risked, launched rare-disease asset, or about $2.55 billion; (2) elegrobart, the under-the-skin follow-on, reaching roughly $600 million of peak sales, discounted for the weaker REVEAL-1 effect size and for approval risk on the planned first-quarter 2027 filing, worth about $0.9 billion; (3) net cash of roughly $790 million (approximately $1.0 billion of cash less the $225 million of 2032 convertible notes). That sums to about $4.24 billion, from which the bull case must fund three to four more years of losses before profitability, worth roughly $0.7 billion, leaving about $3.54 billion. On an as-converted count near 125 million shares that is about $28; on the 110 million common shares alone it is about $32. Call it $30.
sop_bear: About $8.50 a share, and this is an estimate rather than a hard backstop - there is no contract, no deal price and no financing commitment behind it. Built from parts: (1) net cash of roughly $790 million today ($762.2 million at 31 March 2026, plus about $334.7 million of net May offering proceeds, plus the $75 million DRI Healthcare approval milestone, less a launch-weighted quarter of the $104.9 million quarterly loss and a further month, less the $225 million of 2032 convertible notes), which is about $7.20 a share on roughly 110 million common shares and about $6.30 on an as-converted count near 125 million; plus (2) a residual of $2.00 to $2.50 a share for an approved, launched, differentiated rare-disease asset that a strategic buyer would want even if Viridian cannot commercialise it itself. Two things make this floor sturdier than it was in our prior read: the dilutive raise has already been done, at $17.00 in May 2026 before the binary event, so the usual mechanism for breaking a cash floor is off the table for roughly two years; and the notes do not mature until 2032. The offsetting caveat is that the cash half erodes by roughly a dollar a share every two to three quarters at the current burn, so an $8.50 floor today is closer to $7.50 in eighteen months absent revenue.
sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across three commercial outcomes, because the regulatory question is already settled. A 30% weight on a strong launch where infusion sites switch on the shorter course and broader label, coverage arrives inside management's six-to-nine-month guidance, and the follow-on drug is filed and approved on schedule - worth about $30. A 40% weight on an adequate but slow launch where Lumvoa takes a modest share of a $2 billion class from behind the incumbent on formulary and the follow-on is delayed or commercially limited by its weaker effect size - worth about $20. A 30% weight on a poor launch: payers keep Lumvoa behind Tepezza, the ramp disappoints, and the company is marked back toward net cash plus a small strategic residual - worth about $9.50. That weights to roughly $19.85. The parts underneath, in all three cases, are the same three: the approved infused drug (net of a roughly 7.5% U.S. royalty), the under-the-skin follow-on, and roughly $790 million of net cash burning at more than $100 million a quarter - spread across an as-converted count near 125 million shares.
risk_reward: Roughly break-even on the base case and about 0.9 to 1 on the bull case - not the asymmetry this sleeve exists to own. From $19.70 at the 27 July 2026 close: upside to the reconciled base-case value of $19.85 is about 1%; upside to the $30 bull case is about 52%; downside to the $8.50 estimated floor is about 57%. So even the good-launch scenario pays roughly what the bad one costs, and the base case pays nothing. The floor is soft (net cash plus a judgement-based strategic residual, no contract behind it) but it is firmer than our prior read assumed, because the dilutive financing that normally breaks such a floor has already been completed at $17.00 in May 2026.
catalyst_summary: The catalyst has already fired: the FDA approved Lumvoa (veligrotug-vvze) for thyroid eye disease on 26 June 2026, four days ahead of its 30 June target date and with a broader label than expected - and the stock is at $19.70 a month later, so the re-rating we were waiting to be paid for has been spent without paying, leaving roughly 52% upside to a $30 good-launch value against 57% downside to an $8.50 cash-based floor.
dated_milestone: FDA approval granted 26 June 2026 (the target decision date was 30 June 2026) - fired, favourably and early, with the launch beginning the same week. Remaining calendar, none of it hard or binding: second-quarter results expected around 5 August 2026 (a stub month of launch revenue); management's guidance of broad insurance coverage within six to nine months of launch, pointing to roughly December 2026 through March 2027; a company-controlled approval filing for elegrobart targeted for the first quarter of 2027; and a European decision expected during 2027 on the application accepted in February 2026.
forcing_function: There is no longer a hard date that forces a re-rating, and that is the central finding. The nearest scheduled event is second-quarter results around 5 August 2026, but it covers roughly one month of selling against a consensus revenue estimate near $12.5 million, so it can neither settle nor break the question. The real re-rating trigger is a slow-moving commercial one: management has guided to broad insurance coverage within six to nine months of the June launch, which puts the decisive evidence in the fourth-quarter 2026 and first-quarter 2027 reports - the first two periods that will show whether infusion sites are actually switching from Amgen's Tepezza and whether insurers place Lumvoa alongside the incumbent rather than behind it. After that, the next genuine binary is the approval filing for the under-the-skin follow-on targeted for the first quarter of 2027, and that is a submission the company controls, not an agency decision date. A European decision lands sometime in 2027 with no published date.
consensus_delta:
The interesting disagreement here is not between us and the sell side - it is between the sell side and the tape, and the tape is winning. On approval, Wedbush raised its target to $43, Goldman Sachs to $39, Truist to $38 and RBC to $35, with Wells Fargo moving the other way to $26. Seventeen analysts now average $36.13 and the stock trades at $19.70, roughly 45% below it. When targets rise sharply on good news and the price falls anyway, the market is rejecting the models, not handing out a gift.

We think two specific street assumptions are wrong, and one of them is arithmetic rather than judgement.

The first is the bridge from the approved infused drug to the under-the-skin follow-on. Those raised targets are built on a franchise, not a product: they assume elegrobart converts a twelve-week infusion course into a self-administered pen and captures the chronic, long-duration segment where the real money in this disease sits. The 30 March 2026 REVEAL-1 data undercut that. Elegrobart delivered 54% and 63% proptosis response against an unusually high 18% placebo rate at week 24 - a placebo-adjusted gap of roughly 36 to 45 percentage points - against 70% versus 5% at week 15 for the approved drug, a gap of about 64. The market marked the stock down roughly a third that day and has kept it there through an approval. We read that as the correct call.

The second is simpler and, we suspect, an outright modelling lag: the per-share denominator and the royalty. Most published targets were struck on roughly 102 million shares and gross peak sales. Since then the company has issued 7,352,942 shares at $17.00 and $225 million of convertible notes struck at about $24.65 (May 2026), on top of convertible preferred stock worth about 14.3 million common-equivalent shares - a fully diluted count near 134 million, roughly 30% above the base most models use. Separately, about 7.5% of U.S. franchise sales is permanently owed to DRI Healthcare under the October 2025 royalty financing. Neither the extra shares nor the royalty appears to have been pushed through the $36 average. Correct for both and the street's own peak-sales assumptions produce something closer to $30 than $36.

Where we differ from our own prior read is on the setup itself, and on the balance sheet. Our board entry still describes an undated approval decision with a target of $35 and a floor of $8. That decision resolved a month ago. Our earlier note also carried cash near $600 million, having missed the May raise and the $75 million approval milestone; the true figure is roughly $1.0 billion. That correction makes the downside sturdier and the upside thinner at the same time - which is exactly the wrong direction for an asymmetry trade, even though it is the right direction for a business.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are a spending peak against a revenue base starting at zero, with no event capable of settling the argument - but for once the cash is not the binding constraint.

The arithmetic: Viridian lost $104.9 million in the first quarter of 2026 on $141 thousand of revenue, with the full commercial organisation already hired ahead of a launch that had not started. Cash was $762.2 million at 31 March, the May offerings added about $334.7 million net, and the DRI Healthcare approval milestone added $75 million in late June. Net of a launch-weighted second quarter, cash today is roughly $1.0 billion against $225 million of convertible notes that do not mature until 2032 - roughly $790 million net, or about $6.50 to $7.00 a share depending on how the preferred and the notes are counted. At the current burn that is well over two years of runway, and management has said it expects the plan to be funded through profitability.

So the risk in this window is not insolvency; it is the absence of anything good. Management's own guidance is that broad insurance coverage takes six to nine months from the June launch, which means the ramp does not meaningfully begin until roughly December 2026 through March 2027. The second-quarter report around 5 August 2026 contains about one month of selling against a consensus estimate near $12.5 million and cannot reassure anyone. In between, payer decisions may place Lumvoa behind Tepezza on formulary, which in an infused rare-disease market means step-through requirements that slow the ramp for a year; infusion sites have six years of habit and contracting with the incumbent and switch slowly; and Amgen has both the resources and the motive to defend roughly $2 billion of annual demand on price. The plausible bad outcome here is not a financing crisis but two or three quarters of nothing, during which the stock drifts toward its cash while the burn quietly lowers the cash. That is a slow bleed, not a cliff - and a slow bleed is a poor use of a position in a sleeve built for dated events.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling here has largely already happened, which is a point in the stock's favour and the strongest argument for patience rather than purchase.

This shareholder base was event-driven, not yield-focused: crossover biotechnology funds and catalyst traders positioned for the 30 June decision. Three mechanical unwinds have already run through it. The first was 30 March 2026, when the REVEAL-1 data broke the pipeline story and the shares fell roughly a third in a session, flushing the holders underwriting the follow-on drug. The second was deliberate supply: the company itself sold 7,352,942 shares at $17.00 in early May, plus $225 million of convertible notes whose buyers typically short the stock to hedge - real, sustained pressure through the second quarter. The third is the slower one now finishing: the approval on 26 June was the exit event for anyone holding purely for the regulatory outcome, and a full round-trip to $19.70 within a month is the signature of that base handing stock to whoever will take it.

The evidence that this has largely cleared: the shares trade above their 50-day average of $17.66 while sitting far below the 200-day average of $24.03, and comfortably off the $13.18 52-week low. Selling pressure has abated even though the price has not recovered. What has not happened is the buyer rotation - the event funds have left, but the growth and specialty-pharmaceutical funds that would own a commercial-stage launch story generally wait for two quarters of prescription data before building. That gap between seller exhaustion and buyer arrival is exactly where this stock sits, and given management's six-to-nine-month coverage guidance it can persist into the first quarter of 2027. The one genuinely encouraging structural point is that the usual final source of forced supply - an emergency equity raise - has already been taken, at $17.00, before the event rather than after it.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a pass for now, and the reason is simple enough to state in one sentence: we were underwriting a dated regulatory decision, that decision arrived on 26 June 2026 - early, clean, and with a broader label than we expected - and the stock is at $19.70 a month later. When the best available outcome of a binary event does not pay, the market is pricing something the event did not address, and continuing to hold is no longer the trade we sized. It is a different trade wearing the old trade's clothes.

What the market is pricing is the 30 March 2026 data on elegrobart, the under-the-skin follow-on. That trial met its goal but at roughly 36 to 45 placebo-adjusted percentage points against about 64 for the approved infused drug, and the shares fell roughly a third that day and never recovered. The self-administered format is what was supposed to carry a chronic-disease franchise over a decade. A weaker version of it is a smaller company, and an approval for the infused drug does not repair that.

Two corrections to our own file, pulling in opposite directions. First, the balance sheet is much stronger than we carried: the company raised $350 million gross in May 2026 - shares at $17.00 plus 1.75% notes due 2032 - and collected a $75 million approval milestone from its royalty partner in late June, so cash is roughly $1.0 billion, not $600 million. The dilution risk we flagged as the way the floor breaks has already been taken, before the event, which is good treasury discipline and lifts the honest floor to about $8.50 to $9.00. Second, and against that, the same financing and the roughly 7.5% royalty on U.S. franchise sales lower the per-share upside: on a fully diluted count near 134 million and net of the royalty, our own good-launch value is about $30, not the $35 our board carried or the $36.13 the street averages. A firmer floor and a lower ceiling is the wrong direction for an asymmetry trade even when it is the right direction for a business.

None of this makes Viridian a bad company. Strip out roughly $790 million of net cash and the operating business is valued near $1.4 billion against a franchise that might reach $1.4 to $1.5 billion of combined peak sales - not expensive - and the approval is real, differentiated on both dosing burden and label breadth, launched into a market Amgen has already proved is worth about $2 billion a year. But our reconciled base-case value is $19.85, which is where the stock trades. Against 57% downside to a soft cash-based floor, roughly no upside to base case and 52% to the good-launch case is not a trade.

What would change our mind, specifically: the fourth-quarter 2026 and first-quarter 2027 reports showing infusion sites actually switching, combined with broad payer coverage inside management's stated six-to-nine-month window rather than step-through placement behind the incumbent. Alternatively, a price in the low teens - near the cash - would restore the asymmetry that the approval has spent. Until one of those arrives, this belongs off the book.
interrogator_dossier:
# Viridian Therapeutics (VRDN) — event dossier

*Prepared 28 July 2026. Every date and figure below was checked against company releases, regulatory
coverage, the filed first-quarter 2026 financials, the May 2026 offering documents, and a live market
quote on the day of writing.*

## The headline finding

**The event this name was bought for has already happened, it happened early and well, and the stock is
lower a month later.**

Our watch-list entry describes an undated approval decision with a target of $35 and a downside floor of
$8. That entry is stale in the most important way: the decision resolved. The U.S. Food and Drug
Administration approved Viridian's lead drug — Lumvoa (veligrotug-vvze), for thyroid eye disease — on
**26 June 2026**, four days ahead of its 30 June target decision date, with no advisory committee and no
rejection letter. Shares changed hands at **$19.70** at the 27 July 2026 close, against a 52-week range of
$13.18 to $34.29, a 50-day average of $17.66 and a 200-day average of $24.03.

The stock is barely above where it traded the day before the approval. Whatever gap existed between the
live price and the event-resolved value has been settled by the event. What remains is not a special
situation with a hard date and a bounded loss. It is an ordinary, and quite difficult, first-product
commercial launch against an entrenched incumbent.

**One important correction to our own prior read:** the balance sheet is materially stronger than our
earlier note assumed, because that note missed two financings. Viridian raised $350 million gross in
early May 2026 and collected a $75 million approval milestone from a royalty partner in late June. Cash
today is roughly a billion dollars, not the $600 million we previously carried. That raises the floor and
removes the dilution risk we had flagged as the way the floor breaks — but it does not restore the
asymmetry, because it also raised the share count and the price is unchanged.

## 1. Is the catalyst real, dated, and binding?

It was all three, and it is now spent.

| Step | Date | Verified outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Breakthrough therapy designation | 2025 | Granted |
| Application accepted, priority review granted | 22 December 2025 | Target decision date set at 30 June 2026 |
| European application accepted for review | February 2026 | Decision expected during 2027, no date given |
| **U.S. approval of Lumvoa** | **26 June 2026** | **Approved four days early; commercial launch the same week** |

A priority review shortens the agency's clock to roughly six months from acceptance instead of ten. The
agency beat even that. The approved wording is the one management asked for and broader than the base
case: Lumvoa is indicated "for the treatment of thyroid eye disease regardless of thyroid eye disease
activity or duration," making it the first drug in its class carrying clinical data for both the active
and the chronic forms of the disease on its label. The course is five intravenous infusions every three
weeks over about twelve weeks, against the incumbent's eight infusions over roughly 24 weeks. In the
registrational trials, among patients who had double vision at the start, 59% improved and 49% saw it
resolve completely, against 20% and 12% on placebo. The company told physicians they could prescribe the
next day, and priced the course at about $450,000, broadly in line with the incumbent.

**There is no remaining hard, dated, binding regulatory event in front of this stock.** What is left is a
calendar of soft milestones: second-quarter results expected around **5 August 2026** (a stub quarter
covering roughly one month of selling); management's guidance that broad insurance coverage should arrive
within **six to nine months** of launch, which points to roughly December 2026 through March 2027 and is a
company expectation rather than a scheduled event; a planned approval filing for the follow-on drug
**elegrobart in the first quarter of 2027**, which is a submission the company controls, not an agency
decision; and a European decision sometime in 2027.

## 2. How credible is management on hitting dates?

**High on regulatory and operational execution, and better than we credited on treasury management.
Weaker on setting expectations for the pipeline.**

The green flags are dated and checkable. Management said in January 2026 and again with first-quarter
results on 5 May 2026 that the field organisation — sales, market access, patient services — was fully
hired and that manufacturing, distribution and supply chain were launch-ready. When the approval landed on
26 June the company launched immediately. That is a promise made and kept inside six months.

The treasury work deserves more credit than our prior note gave it. On 6 May 2026 — seven weeks before the
approval, and five weeks after the shares had been cut by a third on trial data — Viridian priced two
concurrent offerings: 7,352,942 common shares at $17.00 (about $125 million) and $225 million of 1.75%
convertible senior notes due 2032, convertible at about $24.65 a share, a 45% premium. Aggregate gross
proceeds were $350 million and net proceeds about $334.7 million; the deals closed around 11 May. Raising
into weakness ahead of a binary event is unglamorous, but it means the company did not have to negotiate
from need afterwards. A separate royalty financing with DRI Healthcare, signed in October 2025 for up to
$300 million, delivered a further **$75 million milestone on the approval itself** (confirmed by DRI on
29 June 2026). The price of that money is a tiered royalty of about 7.5% on U.S. sales of the thyroid eye
disease franchise — real, permanent, and a drag on peak economics that most published models understate.

The red flag is **30 March 2026**. Viridian reported topline results from REVEAL-1, the late-stage trial
of elegrobart, the under-the-skin version of the same drug mechanism. The company called the result
positive, and technically it was — the trial met its main goal with high statistical significance. But the
shares fell roughly a third in a single session and have never recovered. The market's objection was
specific and, in my view, correct: investors had been led to expect that because elegrobart hits the same
target as the infused drug, it would reproduce the same effect size. It did not.

| Measure | Veligrotug (infused, approved) | Elegrobart (under the skin) |
|---|---|---|
| Proptosis response, active disease | 70% at week 15 vs 5% placebo | 54% (every four weeks) / 63% (every eight weeks) at week 24 vs 18% placebo |
| Placebo-adjusted gap | about 64 percentage points | about 36 to 45 percentage points |
| Chronic disease | 56% vs 8% placebo | Positive (REVEAL-2, reported second quarter 2026), effect size not matched to the infused drug |

The follow-on drug is the one that was supposed to carry the franchise past its first product, because a
self-administered pen is the format that wins a chronic rare disease over a decade. It works, but it works
less well than the drug it was meant to replace, against a placebo arm that behaved unusually high. That
is an impairment of long-run value, not a sentiment wobble, and it is why an approval three months later
could not lift the stock back.

## 3. What actually backstops the price if the launch disappoints?

Better than our prior note said, but still an estimate rather than a contract.

Verified capital structure and cash:

- Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities at 31 March 2026: **$762.2 million**
- Plus net proceeds of the May offerings: about **$334.7 million**
- Plus the royalty-partner approval milestone in late June: **$75 million**
- Less second-quarter operating burn of roughly $110 to $120 million (the first quarter lost
  $104.9 million on $141 thousand of revenue, with research spending of $77.6 million and selling and
  administrative spending of $38.7 million), and roughly another month since
- **Cash today: approximately $1.0 billion**, against $225 million of convertible notes that do not mature
  until 2032. Net cash is therefore roughly **$790 million**.

Share count: 102,458,094 common shares at 31 March, plus the 7.35 million issued in May, gives roughly
**110 million common shares** today. Convertible preferred stock adds about 14.3 million common-equivalent
shares, taking the as-converted count to roughly 125 million, and the 2032 notes would add about
9.1 million more above $24.65, for a fully diluted count near 134 million.

So net cash is about **$7.20 a share** on the common count, **$6.30** on an as-converted basis, and about
**$7.60** if the notes convert and their principal is extinguished. Call it **$6.50 to $7.00 a share of
genuinely defensible cash**, roughly a third of the current price. That is a real cushion, and because the
raise is already done at $17.00, the mechanism by which a cash floor normally breaks — an emergency equity
issue into a falling price — has largely been taken off the table for the next two years.

On top of the cash sits a residual for the operating business. An approved, launched, differentiated
rare-disease drug with a broader label than a roughly $2 billion incumbent is worth something to a
strategic buyer even if Viridian cannot commercialise it alone. I would put that at $2.00 to $2.50 a
share in a bad-launch scenario. **That gives a downside floor near $8.50 to $9.00** — modestly above the
$8 our board carried, and now more solid than it was. But it remains a judgement, not a backstop: there is
no deal price, no contract and no financing commitment behind it, and the operating business still
consumes more than $100 million a quarter.

## 4. Red flags

**The re-rating already happened and reversed.** Analysts raised targets aggressively on approval —
Wedbush to $43, Goldman Sachs to $39, Truist to $38, RBC to $35, with Wells Fargo moving the other way to
$26. Seventeen analysts now average $36.13 against a $19.70 price. When targets rise sharply on good news
and the price falls anyway, the market is rejecting the models rather than offering a gift.

**The follow-on drug underperformed its own predecessor.** Discussed above. This is the load-bearing
long-term problem.

**A permanent royalty on the franchise.** Roughly 7.5% of U.S. sales of the thyroid eye disease franchise
is owed to a royalty partner. That is the cost of the non-dilutive money, and it comes straight off the
top of every published peak-sales estimate.

**Cash burn against a revenue base starting at zero,** with a fully staffed commercial organisation. The
cash lasts, but every quarter of a slow ramp converts cushion into sunk cost.

**A well-resourced incumbent.** Amgen's Tepezza has had this market to itself since 2020 at roughly
$2 billion of annual demand, with six years of infusion-site relationships and the capacity to defend on
price and contracting.

**Class safety warnings on the label.** Hearing impairment including potentially permanent hearing loss,
raised blood sugar in about 12% of trial patients, infusion reactions in about 9%, and inflammatory bowel
disease. These are class effects shared with the incumbent, so they are not a competitive disadvantage —
but they do cap how fast prescribing broadens beyond specialist centres.

## 5. Green flags

**A clean, early approval with a broader label than the incumbent** — the first drug approved for this
disease regardless of how active or long-standing it is.

**A shorter treatment course** — five infusions over about twelve weeks against eight over roughly 24. For
a patient in an infusion chair, and for the clinic scheduling those chairs, that is a visible advantage
rather than a statistical one.

**The market already exists.** Physicians recognise the disease, insurers pay for the class, and infusion
economics are settled. Viridian is competing for demand, not creating it.

**The balance sheet is funded and the dilution is behind it.** Roughly a billion dollars of cash, raised
opportunistically before the event, against notes that mature in 2032.

**The follow-on drug did work.** Both late-stage trials met their goals and the approval filing is on
track for the first quarter of 2027. It is a weaker drug than hoped, not a failed one.

## 6. What the director must weigh

This name entered our process as a dated approval decision with a wide gap between the price and the
event-resolved value. That description is no longer true, and the honest thing is to say so rather than
re-tell the story with the launch quietly substituted for the approval.

The approval fired favourably, early, and with a better label than the base case — the best available
version of the event we were underwriting — and the stock is unchanged to lower a month later. When the
good outcome of a binary event does not pay, the market is pricing something the event did not address.
Here that something is the March data on the follow-on drug, plus honest doubt about how quickly a second
entrant takes share from an entrenched incumbent through payer contracting.

What is left is a reasonable but ordinary commercial-stage biotechnology company. Strip out roughly
$790 million of net cash and the operating business carries an enterprise value near $1.4 billion, against
a franchise that might reach $1.4 to $1.5 billion of combined peak annual sales before a 7.5% royalty. That
is not expensive. It is also not a defined-risk asymmetric setup with a hard date, which is what this
sleeve exists to own. On my own build the shares are worth roughly $20 on probability-weighted odds —
essentially where they trade — with about $30 in a good launch and $8.50 to $9.00 if the launch fails.

The next genuinely informative moment is not a date but a data series: the fourth-quarter 2026 and
first-quarter 2027 reports, which will show whether infusion sites are actually switching and whether
insurers put Lumvoa alongside the incumbent rather than behind it.

On durability, mostly beside the point for an event name but for completeness: the protection is
regulatory — patent and biologic exclusivity on an approved product — which is real but narrow in a class
where the incumbent is Amgen and at least one under-the-skin format is coming. No structural force
threatens the terminal value of treating this disease; the risk is competitive, not secular.
